title: Cape Cod Bay Meteorite Fall Zone Mapped by Researchers
excerpt: That fireball over Cape Cod in May? Scientists just mapped where its pieces likely fell into the bay.
content:
A blinding daytime fireball tore across the Massachusetts coast on May 30, 2026, ending its violent plunge over Cape Cod Bay with a sonic boom heard across the region. Five months later, an international team of scientists has reconstructed the object's path through the solar system and pinpointed roughly where its surviving pieces likely came to rest beneath the waves.

The object has been classified as a superbolide, meaning an exceptionally bright meteor, according to The Boston Globe, which reported that scientists and researchers from around the globe reconstructed the meteor's origins and its path before it entered Earth's atmosphere. The Globe reports that before atmospheric entry, the object measured about 5 feet across and weighed roughly 12,000 pounds, barreling into the atmosphere at nearly 58,000 miles per hour. A new study, published in The Astronomical Journal, describes the event as exceptionally rare.

Piecing Together a Fireball's Final Seconds

To reconstruct what happened, researchers leaned on a dense web of sensors. Per the Globe's reporting, the team used meteor radar, conventional weather radar, satellite observations, and nearly 200 atmospheric pressure sensors to track the shock waves the meteor generated as it broke apart. Separately, a study hosted on arxiv.org notes that weather-radar detections helped refine the dark-flight solution and place the likely fall region in Cape Cod Bay, while CBS Boston adds that the reconstruction also drew on dashcam and security video, four weather radars, and the MIT Haystack Observatory's specular radar.

That mix of sensors wasn't just academic. The fireball was captured on a security camera as far away as Mechanicville, New York, north of Albany, on the same day it lit up skies over Massachusetts. The arxiv.org study further reports that radar observations localized short-lived plasma-wake echoes down to roughly 30 kilometers in altitude, which the researchers identify as the radar terminus, the point where the object's breakup was expected to occur.

A Dense, Iron-Rich Traveler With a Murky Past

What survived long enough to reach that altitude appears to have been unusually tough. The radar and dark-flight evidence are consistent with a dense, mechanically strong meteoroid, possibly iron-rich, according to the arxiv.org study, and the Globe similarly reports the object was likely rich in iron and unusually dense and mechanically strong.

Where it came from is less certain. The Globe reports the meteor likely originated from an asteroid or comet somewhere in Jupiter's orbit, with an average solar distance of about 227 million miles compared with Earth's average of 93 million miles, and that at its farthest point it reached about 4.27 times Earth's distance from the sun. But the arxiv.org study is more cautious about pinning down a category: backward propagation of the trajectory places the object's heliocentric orbit near the boundary between cometary and asteroidal classifications, with empirical dynamical criteria producing conflicting results. Catalogue comparisons, the study adds, identified no convincing parent body or established meteor-shower association.

Fragments Possibly Resting Near the Bay's Center

Researchers believe fragments likely survived their fiery descent and landed in Cape Cod Bay, according to the Globe, which reports they are estimated to lie within a 1.9-by-2.3-mile area near the bay's center, where the water reaches a maximum depth of around 200 feet. Some models cited by the Globe suggest individual fragments could weigh anywhere from a few ounces to around 3 pounds.

Energy estimates for the blast vary depending on the method and source. The arxiv.org study says regional infrasound data independently supports the terminal fragmentation region and yields an energy estimate of 0.5 kilotons of TNT equivalent, while NASA's independent estimate, cited by the Globe, put the released energy at 1.1 kilotons. That figure has also shifted in earlier reporting: a June Boston Globe report said NASA had initially estimated the event released energy equivalent to about 230 tons of TNT. The arxiv.org study notes that only three events in NASA's CNEOS catalogue for all of 2025 had estimated impact energies exceeding the 1.1-kiloton figure later reported for the Cape Cod Bay bolide, and compares the blast to the 1.2-kiloton 2008 TC3 asteroid impact over Sudan, as well as to roughly a quarter of the energy released during the 4-kiloton Sutter's Mill event.

Rare for New England, Routine for the Planet

Events like this aren't unheard of globally, even if they rarely touch down so close to a populated coastline. MIT planetary scientist Richard Binzel told the Boston Globe that similar meteor events happen regularly around the world, often over remote oceans where nobody notices. A report from theskyscrapers.org noted that late May is typically one of the quieter stretches of the year for meteor activity, and that the Cape Cod bolide didn't appear tied to any known meteor stream.

The same report placed the event in a short recent run of notable American fireballs, pointing to similar bolides reported earlier in 2026 over Texas and Ohio, and noting that it had been several years since one fell over the northeastern United States, dating back to a 2023 event in remote eastern Maine. For Cape Cod, at least, the mystery of exactly what rests on the bay floor remains unresolved even as scientists narrow in on where to look.
